the rate of healing and the amount of callus formed in patients with head injury and femoral fractures is greater than in patients with femoral fractures without head injury.
the rate of callus formation and the time to union of femoral fractures were significantly greater in patients with head injury than in patients with similar fractures and no associated head injury.

In a group of patients who had suffered a severe head injury and who subsequently developed a femoral fracture, the fracture healed more rapidly and with more callus than did a control group with femoral fractures but without head injury."

the study of the healing of fractures of the femoral diaphysis in patients with associated head injury.
the development and application of novel materials, methods and devices for the treatment of fractures and bone defects.
the development of an experimental model of the human femoral fracture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in patients who have sustained severe head injuries, fractures of the lower limbs heal more quickly and with more callus formation than in those without head injury.

the presence of head injuries in patients with femoral fractures does not influence the healing process in the latter, but that the presence of femoral fractures may have a deleterious effect on the course of recovery from head injuries.

, in patients in whom the head injury is severe enough to cause a prolonged period of unconsciousness, there will be a tendency for excessive callus to form and the rate of fracture healing will be faster than normal, although the latter may be difficult to assess.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the head-injured patient, the fracture should be treated in the usual way, but that the surgeon should be prepared to deal with complications which are more likely to occur.

, in patients in whom the head injury is not severe and who are treated with a nail, there are no differences in the healing of the fracture between the two groups, but, when the head injury is severe and the patient is treated with a nail or with traction, there is an increased incidence of nonunion and delayed healing.
, in patients without head injuries, the callus is more compact and less extensive than that in patients with associated head injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rate of callus formation and healing is not related to the degree of head injury.
we can use this information to help us understand the mechanisms that underlie the development of callus in patients with head injury.
the callus is a very important structure for fracture healing.
